frictions: Four review rounds, every one finding something real. The recurring class was never the code and never the intent — it was a claim about coverage that the coverage did not support. Round 2's was the sharpest: a scripted edit whose anchor no longer matched, and Python silently does nothing when the pattern is absent, so the brief asserted a fix with byte-identical code behind it.

Round 3's fix (report_once) shipped with zero coverage because the existing stub refuses EVERY request, so documentSymbol fails, no functions are extracted, and the site under test is never reached. A stub that is too aggressive is indistinguishable from a stub that works, and the test still passes.

methods: Mutation as the unit of proof: 21 mutants, 20 killed, each run through the command the report cites. The one survivor is documented as a survivor.
Assert the anchor of every scripted edit. One assertion fired and caught a no-op edit.
Counts, not containments, whenever the property IS the number. contains cannot tell 3 from 126.
Bound a delta by what CANNOT have changed: 3292 edges outside the touched file were raw-byte-identical, which bounds the golden's +2 without trusting any normalisation.

suggestion: roster-qa should hard-verify its toolchain before running any gate, and be forbidden from returning NO-GO on a missing-dependency error without first printing proof that the environment was right. A missing library is an environment diagnosis, not a verdict on a branch — and an agent that converts one into the other produces exactly the false red that trains people to bypass gates.

frictions: Three successive root-cause diagnoses were wrong, and each was 'proven' by a measurement that could not have shown otherwise. exec_stmt was fail-open: it printed on any non-DONE step and continued, so a run could lose 1835 rows and still exit 0. The investigation could not have converged without first making the producer fail closed — the instrument had to be repaired before it could measure.
methods: Instrumented the insert path to count re-inserts by (module, name) rather than reasoning about which shapes could collide: 96 re-inserts across exactly 4 pairs, all <module>|_, all from [@@deriving] sentinels. The count is what decided the fix.
Reduced to a 3-line ppx fixture showing 15 reported / 3 stored (80% loss), then a second fixture using top-level shadowing to show the cascade is not specific to `_`.

Distinguished at source vs after ppx: `_` is Tpat_any and already fell through (verified empirically); a ppx forges an Ident named "_" because Ident.t has no validation. The string comparison is therefore not a shortcut past a structural test — the ppx erased the structure.
suggestion: roster-investigate should require every refutation to name the stream and the binary it was measured on. Two of my three wrong diagnoses came from grepping the wrong stream (stdout for a stderr message) or running the wrong executable — not from bad reasoning. A 'refuted' verdict whose evidence is a zero count should have to state what a non-zero would have looked like.

methods: Made the producer fail closed in the same change as the fix: a run with rejected statements now exits non-zero and says the counts are ATTEMPTS, not stored rows. On its first real use it caught a 1835-statement cascade on epure that would previously have exited 0.

Staged explicitly by filename and verified with `git diff --cached --numstat | awk '$1=="-"'` before every commit thereafter.
suggestion: A pre-commit check that refuses any staged blob over ~1 MB unless explicitly allowlisted. Prose in a brief did not stop me; a deny-rule would have. The repo's own escalation guidance already argues exactly this — declarative rules need mechanical backing.

frictions: Committed the completed fix directly onto local `main` instead of a feature branch — forgot to `git checkout -b` before implementing. A real near-miss: that work was gone from the working tree with no git object ever created for the exact reset moment, and was only recoverable because it had been git-stash-pushed-and-popped earlier in the session, leaving a dangling stash commit findable via `git fsck --unreachable`. Recovered in full and verified byte-identical to the pre-reset diff, but this should never have been possible to get into.

the general lesson: `git reset --hard` discards uncommitted changes to TRACKED files with no recovery path unless they were staged, stashed, or committed at some point — untracked files survive, tracked-but-modified files do not. Before any hard reset, always check git status first and stash -u anything uncommitted, even when the reset target is believed to only affect commits you made yourself.

suggestion: before running `git reset --hard` for any reason, always run `git status --porcelain` first and stash -u anything present, even when confident the reset is scoped to a commit boundary and not working-tree state — the two are not the same thing and conflating them is exactly how this happened
